keyVerseText: And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. I have: or, I would slay a man in my wound, etc to my hurt: or, in my hurt
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun פֶּצַע (petsaʻ) derives from the root פָּצַע (pâtsaʻ), which fundamentally means 'to split' or 'to wound by bruising or crushing.' This root conveys not only the physical act of inflicting injury but also the resultant state of being wounded or bruised. The literal sense of breaking or splitting adds a vivid dimension to the English gloss 'wound,' emphasizing the rupture or damage inflicted beneath the surface, beyond mere external harm.
usageInScripture: The word פֶּצַע appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, consistently translated with terms related to wounds or bruises, such as 'for wound,' 'to my wounding,' and 'my wounds.' Its usage spans both literal and figurative contexts, indicating physical injury as well as metaphorical or emotional hurt, as seen in translations like 'in it but wounds.' This consistency reveals the term’s core emphasis on injury, whether physical or symbolic, underscoring the reality of brokenness in human experience.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פֶּצַע as a term rooted in the idea of a deep, splitting wound enriches our grasp of human frailty and sin’s effects in Scripture. It reminds believers that sin and suffering are not superficial but deeply penetrating, causing real damage to the soul and body. Christ’s redemptive work addresses these wounds fully, offering healing that restores what was broken by sin. Recognizing the severity of these 'wounds' also calls the Christian to compassion and reliance on God’s grace for restoration and wholeness.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 4:23, Lamech speaks of having slain a man 'to my wounding,' using פֶּצַע to express a deep personal injury or hurt connected to his violent actions. The word highlights not only the physical violence but also the internal damage or consequence he associates with this act. This usage reflects the profound reality that sin and violence injure more than the body—they leave lasting marks on the conscience and community, underscoring the tragic effects of human rebellion.
